readingInstruction: Read 1 Corinthians 11:1-34. The chapter has two parts: guidance on worship conduct (verses 2-16) and the Lord’s Supper (verses 17-34). You read about the Supper yesterday. Today give attention to verses 2-16, which are some of the hardest in the letter to interpret, and read them with humility.
settingTheScene: Paul begins a new section on public worship. He first praises them for remembering him and holding to the traditions as he delivered them. Then he addresses a problem in worship that involved how men and women dressed or wore their hair when praying or prophesying. The details of the first-century practice are not entirely clear to us, which is why interpreters have differed for centuries. What is clear is that both men and women prayed and prophesied in the gathered church, and that Paul cared about order and about honoring Christ.
observation: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (11:1).
“Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman” (11:11).
“If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God” (11:16).
“When you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you” (11:18).
“Each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk” (11:21).
“For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you” (11:23).
“This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me” (11:25).
“When you come together to eat, wait for one another” (11:33).
interpretation:
The chapter opens with a command that belongs to the previous section: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.” Then Paul commends them for keeping the traditions. “But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.” The word translated “head” (kephale) is debated. Some understand it as authority, leading to a view that men have a leading role in the home and church. Others understand it as source or origin, since the passage speaks of woman coming from man in creation. Christians who love the Bible land in different places, so we should be gracious.

Paul then gives instructions about heads being covered or uncovered when praying or prophesying. It is likely that the issue was cultural markers of honor and shame in Corinth, and that Paul wanted men and women to present themselves in a way that did not bring disgrace or confusion about the gender distinctions God made. Some churches have taken this passage as requiring head coverings for women today; others see the principle as honoring order and distinction while the specific custom was cultural. Paul himself says, “We have no such practice, nor do the churches of God,” for those who are contentious. What is beyond dispute is verse 11: “In the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman; for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.” Men and women need one another, and both are from God. And Paul assumes that women pray and prophesy in the assembly.

Verses 17 to 34 return to the Lord’s Supper, which you studied yesterday. Paul says the divisions among them are in a sense necessary “in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized.” Their meal was becoming a display of status. “Do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing?” This is a rebuke of the rich who eat first. Paul then recalls the Lord’s own words. The Supper is a proclamation of the cross and a call to unity.

Self-examination and discerning the body (the church) are both required. The weak and sick among them show the seriousness of misusing the meal. Paul’s practical conclusion is simple: “So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that when you come together it will not be for judgment.”

The big idea of the chapter is that worship is ordered by the gospel. Whatever our practice, it must honor Christ, build up the church, and care for the weak.
connection: Genesis 1:26-27 and 2:18-23 are the creation background. Ephesians 5:21-33 speaks of headship and love. Galatians 3:28 says there is no male and female in Christ. Acts 2:17-18 and 21:9 mention women prophesying. 1 Timothy 2:8-15 also addresses worship. Luke 22:19-20 is the institution of the Supper. 1 Corinthians 10:16-17 speaks of participation. James 2:1-9 warns against partiality toward the rich. Hebrews 13:7 says to imitate the faith of leaders. Philippians 2:3-4 urges us to look to the interests of others.
application:
Ask whom in your church gets overlooked. Wait for them, honor them, and include them.

Pray that your church’s worship would reflect the gospel in both order and love.

On a point where Christians disagree, ask how you can listen first.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to help you imitate those who imitate Christ.
Ask him to order your worship.
Thank him for making men and women for one another.
